title: Gumbel Distillation for Parallel Text Generation
claim: A teacher's sampling, with its noise recorded, yields (sequence, noise) pairs, and a parallel student trained on those pairs learns the joint distribution.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right: dashed zoom-in inset, Stage 1 data generation, Stage 2 student training. Color legend at top right, dashed zoom connector.
description: A wide three-part diagram with a legend at top right: gray for tokens, green for logits, yellow for Gumbel noise. The left panel, in a dashed orange box, is a zoomed-in view of Gumbel-Max sampling. Green logit bars and yellow noise bars are summed through a plus node, producing stacked bars. An argmax arrow then points to a single gray token. The middle panel, 'Stage 1: Data Generation', shows an AR Teacher block p*(x^i | x^<i). It feeds logits l^1..l^n upward. Each logit is combined with a noise node ξ^i to give a token x^i. A dashed gray arrow feeds x^1 back as the next input, starting from BOS. The right panel, 'Stage 2: Student Training', shows a Parallel Student block taking x^¬I and ξ^I. It predicts logits l̂^I, which are compared with the target tokens x^I through a CE Loss arrow. Blue arrows and rounded boxes carry the flow, and the eye goes first to the stage titles.
caption: A conceptual overview of \oursnew. The distillation process consists of two steps: (1) Data Generation: An autoregressive teacher model's sampling process is combined with Gumbel noise to deterministically generate pairs of token sequences and their corresponding Gumbel noise. In practice, one could alternatively extract $\{\xi\}$ in parallel based on an offline training corpus (Section [ref]); (2) Student Training: A parallel student model is trained to predict a target subset of tokens, conditioned on both the context and the Gumbel noise from the teacher.
abstract: The slow, sequential nature of autoregressive (AR) language models has driven the adoption of parallel decoding methods. However, these non-AR models often sacrifice generation quality as they struggle to model the complex joint distribution of token sequences. To narrow this performance gap, we introduce Gumbel Distillation, a novel distillation technique that enables parallel decoders to learn this distribution effectively. Our method leverages the Gumbel-Max trick to create a deterministic mapping from a latent Gumbel noise space to the output tokens of a high-performing AR teacher. As a model-agnostic technique, Gumbel Distillation seamlessly integrates with diverse parallel decoding architectures, including MDLM and BD3-LM. Experiments on LM1B and OpenWebText show that Gumbel Distillation substantially improves the generation quality of parallel language models, achieving a 30.0% improvement in MAUVE score and 10.5% in generative perplexity over MDLM trained on OpenWebText dataset. Code available at https://github.com/hxixixh/gumbel-distill.
